title: Landscape: the whole picture, in order
subtitle: Three research rounds and a decoding panel, reorganized into one story you can read from start to finish: the pressure, the response, the players, the rails, the anchors, energy, work, the next generation, the rivals, the hidden links, and the most likely road to 2050.
intro: The Desk page is the evidence room. It holds every claim this project tested, with its source, its tier and its status. But it was written in the order the research happened, so the findings arrive the way a detective finds clues: out of sequence, with the big picture only visible at the end. This page is the detective's summing-up. It takes everything the Desk knows and lays it out as one story.

The story has a simple spine. The United States carries a debt that grows on its own. Washington is managing it, not shrinking it, by deciding who must buy it. New digital money is being built on top of the old system rather than replacing it. Gold is quietly gaining a job between nations. Energy is taking over the job gold used to do as the real limit on what money can buy. And underneath all of it, ownership, not income, is what decides who keeps up as robots and AI arrive.

Every number here comes from the project's own research files, dated 2026-10-22. Every claim keeps its status: Confirmed, Plausible, Speculative or Refuted, and for claims about hidden intent, a decoded grade from D1 (strong) to D4 (debunked). Where we do not know, we say so. This is general research to help you think, not financial advice.
howToRead: Read in order the first time. Chapters 2 and 3 set up the pressure and the response, and everything later leans on them.

Watch the status words. Confirmed means money moved or a law says so. Plausible means officials' words or market prices plus a working mechanism. Speculative means only commentary supports it. Refuted means hard evidence contradicts it.

Decoded grades are about intent, not outcome. D1 means several independent decoders agree and actions fit. D2 means partial fit. D3 means folklore resting on one source or vibes. D4 means debunked by hard evidence.
Chapter 11 is the shortcut for curious readers. It lists the links between areas that are easy to miss when each topic is read on its own.
The epilogue in Chapter 12 tells the most likely story from now to 2050, with the fork points that would change it.

chapters.title: The question and how we answered it
chapters.kicker: A hunch about Washington, Tokyo and Paris became a test of how to find intent that nobody announces.

blocks.text: This project started with a post on X and a gut feeling. The post claimed that US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had quietly arranged for France to take an economic hit so that Japan could be rescued, as part of a plan to manage a US debt of about $40 trillion. The owner of this project believed it: "Bessent sold France to help Japan... This is about to come (just hasn't priced in yet)." He asked an AI what it thought.

The AI answered the way most careful answers do. It checked the facts it could find, noted there was no public statement from Bessent admitting any such plan, and concluded the idea was "speculative rather than established fact." Then the owner pasted in a long transcript from an expert, Jack Mallers, who laid out a detailed theory. The AI read it and mostly agreed with him. Both answers had the same flaw. The first stopped at "unproven". The second borrowed someone else's frame without checking it.
Why "unproven" is never the end

People in power rarely announce their intent. A finance minister will not say "we are pushing the cost onto Europe." If you only accept official words as proof, the answer to every question about intent will always be "unproven", which tells you nothing. The project's diagnosis listed seven failure modes, and the first one was exactly this: a fact-check frame that ranks official statements on top, when where money actually moved should outrank what anyone says.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: A detective does not wait for a confession. She asks what the suspect would normally have done, notices what he did instead, and follows the money. The odd choice is the clue. In this case the odd choice was simple: when the US helped Japan defend the yen on 31 July 2026, it sold euros, not dollars. Every modern US intervention before that had sold dollars. That one detail was the story.
The method: seven moves and an evidence ladder

From that lesson the project built a Revealed Intent Engine. Every agent runs seven moves: spot the anomaly, state the default move, map incentives, read the actor's history, build the mechanism chain, test it with data, and separate fact from inference with a confidence number.

blocks.caption: The evidence ladder. T0 is money that actually moved, T1 is law, T2 is officials on the record, T3 is market prices, T4 is specialists, T5 is commentary. When sources disagree, the higher tier decides.

blocks.text: The calibration test: did the engine beat the expert?

Before trusting the engine, the project gave it only the raw X post, with no expert transcript, and asked it to work the case. It rebuilt the expert's key anomaly on its own (euros sold, not dollars) and then went further. Treasury's own fund statement showed the US share of the operation was about $500 million, against Japan's roughly ¥15.4 trillion (about $97 billion). Bessent's photographed desk note had said "$5-10 bil". The France to Germany bond spread was flat in August (78 to 82 basis points) and only blew out from mid-September (87 on 10 September to 157.5 on 21 October), after the Fed hike, the Bank of Japan hike, a French budget fight and oil above $100.

items: The literal claim, "Bessent sold France", is Refuted (85). A $500 million euro sale cannot sink a market of about €3.3 trillion of French debt, and the timing does not fit.
A narrow version is Plausible (50). The US chose a funding currency and a policy mix that pushed the cost of rescuing the yen toward the euro area rather than onto the dollar or Treasuries.
"Not priced in yet" is Refuted. By October the short Europe trade was described by UBS and Allianz as crowded.

blocks.text: The signal was the instrument. A photographed note, "I am the house now", and talk of "asymmetric information" moved markets far more than the half a billion dollars that actually changed hands. When an official's words are loud and the money is small, the words are the tool. That gap between saying and doing, recorded for every major actor, turned out to be the most valuable data in the whole project.
Three rounds and a decoding panel

items: Round 0 calibrated the method on the France case.
Round 1 asked the big question: will energy (watts, tonnage, compute) replace the role gold, then bonds, then credit played? Seven research lanes fed four debate courts and a ledger of 419 claims.
Round 2 answered the owner's ten follow-up questions on new money rails, a Universal High Income (UHI), the route for an 18-year-old, founders, and rivals.
Round 3 tested Round 2 against a year of hard data, and a decoding panel graded what Trump, Musk and the advocates of a "reset" really want.

blocks.text: The time frames and the four endings

The project uses four horizons: H0 is now to 2028, H1 is 2028 to 2035, H2 is 2035 to 2050, and H3 is a post-scarcity world after that. It scores four possible regimes for how the money system will look at the end of each horizon: S1 dollar extension (stablecoins and tokenized Treasuries carry the dollar onto new rails), S2 neutral reserve layer (gold and possibly Bitcoin settle between nations), S3 energy or compute standard, and S4 disorderly reset (a crisis or overt repression comes first).

These are judgment odds (Speculative by the project's own rules). Each row sums to 100 and names the regime that best describes the system at the end of that horizon. The scenarios can overlap: S1 plumbing can be the tool of an S4 squeeze.

blocks.q: Why did the project treat the euro sale as more important than Bessent's public statements?
blocks.a: Because it was money that actually moved (T0), and it broke the default pattern: every modern US intervention had sold dollars. An action that breaks a habit tells you more than words that can be chosen for effect.

chapters.title: The pressure: the debt treadmill
chapters.kicker: The US debt grows on its own, mainly because the government spends more than it taxes even before paying interest.

blocks.text: Everything in this story starts with one pressure. The US government owes $40.44 trillion in total, and $32.566 trillion of that is held by the public, about 100% of the economy's yearly output (GDP). In the fiscal year that ended on 30 September 2026 it collected $5,403.3 billion, spent $7,395.8 billion, and borrowed the difference: $1,992.5 billion, about 6.2% of GDP.

Two numbers inside that deficit matter most. Interest on the debt cost $1,051.8 billion. And the rest, the gap between what the government spends on everything else and what it collects, was $940.7 billion, or 2.92% of GDP. Economists call that second number the primary deficit. It is the engine of the whole problem.

blocks.caption: The debt treadmill. The belt is the interest cost, the runner's legs are real growth, and the steady push is the primary deficit. Ways off: spend less, grow faster, or let inflation shrink the debt.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Imagine running on a treadmill while someone keeps adding weight to your backpack. The belt speed is the interest rate on your debt. Your legs are economic growth. The backpack is the primary deficit, new borrowing every year just to cover normal spending. Mallers framed the problem as belt versus legs. The project found the bigger issue is the backpack.
The surprising finding: it is the backpack, not the belt

The popular story says high interest rates are what make the debt explode. The project tested that with Treasury's own numbers. The real interest rate on 10-year debt (2.76%, the yield on inflation-protected bonds) is only slightly above the economy's trend real growth (2.50% a year over ten years). The gap is just +0.26 percentage points. At market rates, the primary deficit explains 92% to 102% of the yearly rise in the debt ratio. Ruling Dc-02: Confirmed, 80.

blocks.text: Repricing: why the bill keeps rising even if nothing changes

The debt is not one loan. It is a pile of loans with expiry dates. Each time one expires, the Treasury borrows again at today's rate. The average rate on the whole pile is 3.518%, but new borrowing costs about 4.88%. Because 70.4% of the marketable debt reprices within five years, the interest bill climbs on its own. If yields hold, the project's model has interest heading to about $1.6 trillion in three years and $1.9 trillion in five.

The Treasury has been funding itself more with short-term bills, which now make up 22.36% of marketable debt. That keeps costs down when short rates are low, but it means every Fed hike passes through to the federal budget within months. Shortening the debt is a bet that short rates will fall. It makes the budget more sensitive, not less.
Was the Fed's hike "gasoline on the fire"?

Mallers argued that when the Fed raises rates, it pays more interest into the economy, so hiking is stimulus. The project checked the size. A quarter-point hike costs about $20 billion to $26 billion a year, about 2% of net interest. The real policy rate is mild: about +0.2% on 12-month inflation of 3.7%. And his inputs were overstated: the debt reprices from 3.52% to about 4.9%, not from 2% to 5%. Ruling Dc-07: the "gasoline" claim is Refuted, 70. The deeper point cuts the other way: a Fed that hikes against the President is evidence against fiscal dominance, not for it.
The quiet helper: inflation

blocks.caption: A shrinking yardstick. Debt is written in dollars, and when prices rise faster than the interest rate on the debt, the real burden shrinks without anyone voting for it.

blocks.text: Here is the part almost nobody says out loud. Nominal growth (real growth plus inflation) is running about 5.7% to 6%, while the average cost of the debt is about 3.2% to 3.5%. That gap quietly holds the debt ratio's drift to about 0.4 to 0.6 points a year. The project calls this passive inflation doing the stabilizing work (Dc-09, Plausible, 60). It fades as the debt reprices. And if inflation fell back to 2% while real rates stayed near 2.7%, the ratio would climb faster, which is a strange truth: success against inflation makes the debt math harder.
Can AI growth fix it?

Elon Musk has said only AI and robots can solve the US debt. The word "only" is Refuted (70): a primary adjustment of about 2.9% of GDP would stabilize the ratio, and history shows growth, inflation, repression and discipline doing the work, never technology alone. But AI can help under three conditions (Dc-03, Confirmed as arithmetic, 75):

items: Spending must not rise with the growth. In the project's model, +2.26 points of AI growth with spending held takes the debt to 87% of GDP. If spending scales up with it, 107%.

Real interest rates must not rise with growth. If they rise one for one, the debt reaches about 129%, the same as with no AI at all. In 2026 the real 10-year yield rose 82 basis points, so this condition is already under strain.
The gains must land in taxable income. In FY2026 corporate receipts fell 15.6%, from $452.1B to $381.4B, as firms deducted AI investment faster. This condition is failing now.

blocks.myth: Money printing has a hard ceiling, and the US is nearly maxed out.
blocks.reality: There is no fixed ceiling. The real limits are the primary deficit, the real interest rate and how much inflation the public will tolerate. The debt can grow for a long time. What changes is who pays, and how visibly.

blocks.q: If the Fed cut rates to zero tomorrow, would the debt problem be solved?
blocks.a: No. Interest costs would fall over time, but the primary deficit of about 2.9% of GDP would keep adding debt every year. The backpack stays even if the belt slows.

chapters.title: The response: how Washington is managing it
chapters.kicker: They are not shrinking the debt. They are managing who must buy it.

blocks.text: Faced with the treadmill, a government has a short menu: tax more, spend less, grow faster, inflate, default, or make sure there are always buyers for the debt. Washington's revealed choice, read from where money actually moved, is the last one. The project calls it captive demand: write rules and build plumbing so that banks, money funds, stablecoin issuers and foreign governments end up holding Treasury bills. Ruling Db-01: Confirmed, 75.
The captive demand toolkit

items: Fund with bills. Coupon auction sizes are frozen with guidance to stay that way for several quarters, and the bill share rose to 22.36% ($7.118 trillion), from 21.53% a year earlier. The refunding statement itself talks about sizing bills to private and Fed demand.
Free up bank balance sheets. The enhanced supplementary leverage ratio (eSLR) relief lets banks hold more Treasuries.
Write bills into the law of digital money. From 2027-01-18 every compliant US stablecoin must hold cash, deposits or Treasury bills of 93 days or less (the GENIUS Act).
Buy back long bonds. Treasury bought back $230 billion of older debt in 2026, funded with bills.
Keep foreign holders from dumping. Press Japan to borrow against its Treasuries through the Fed's FIMA repo line instead of selling, and support the yen with euros rather than with dollars.

blocks.text: Just as President Abraham Lincoln's National Currency Act of 1863 established a national framework for bank-issued currency, the GENIUS Act establishes a federal framework for payment stablecoins in the digital age.

The analogy is the tell. Under the 1863 law, national banks issued notes that had to be backed by federal bonds, which created a permanent buyer for Civil War debt. Bessent names the framework, not the bond backing, so this is intent evidence of moderate weight. But the decoding panel graded "stablecoins as a deliberate captive demand tool for Treasury bills" D1 (80), partly because the Treasury Secretary chose that comparison himself.
What the 2026 stress test showed
Round 3 checked the toolkit against a year of hard data, and the results corrected some of the project's own earlier lines. Three surprises stand out.

items: Stablecoins did not carry the load. Total supply went from $304.9 billion (2025-10-21) to $303.8 billion (2026-10-22), flat for a year after a May peak of $315.5 billion. Over the same year bank deposits rose $1,225 billion, money funds about $505 billion to $7.92 trillion, and the Fed's own bill holdings $370 billion to $565.5 billion. In 2026 the real captive buyers were the Fed and money funds, not tokens.

The crisis line went unused. The Fed's FIMA repo facility was at zero every week from 18 February to 14 October 2026, apart from a $3.0 billion blip on 4 February. Japan said on 3 August it "plans to utilize" FIMA, then did not. Swap lines peaked at $481 million.

Foreign governments sold instead. Foreign official Treasuries in Fed custody fell $254 billion (9.1%) from the February peak to $2,549.1 billion, while those holders kept $331.9 billion of their own cash at the Fed. Japan spent ¥27.1 trillion on interventions in 2026.

blocks.caption: The dollar recycling loop. Dollars sent abroad come back as purchases of Treasuries. In 2026 part of that loop ran in reverse: official holders sold $254 billion to raise crisis cash.

blocks.text: So the project reworded its own summary. FIMA moved from "chosen tool" to "announced but unused" (R3X-03, Confirmed). The holder base has shifted from steady foreign governments to leveraged, price-sensitive private buyers such as basis traders, money funds and stablecoins (Db-12, Confirmed, 80). That keeps the system working in good weather and makes it more fragile in a funding shock.
The Gulf asked, then borrowed

The UAE asked for a dollar swap line in April, and Bessent said "numerous" Gulf and Asian allies had asked. No Gulf line had been announced by 22 October. Gulf states instead issued a record $102.7 billion of bonds and sukuk in the first half of 2026. The court's reading: the backstop for non-core states is moving from the Fed's technical lines to Treasury's political ones, which buys loyalty but makes access conditional and nudges states toward gold and self-insurance.
The Fed under Warsh: hiking, not helping

The Fed raised its rate 12-0 on 2026-09-16 to 3.75% to 4.00%, its first hike since 2023. The President wanted rates "near 1% or lower." Markets on 22 October gave an October hike only 11% to 12% and a December 9 hike 75% to 79%, with year-end rates most likely at 4.25%. Warsh being out as chair by mid-2027 was priced at 9.5%. The Supreme Court kept Governor Cook in June. In plain terms, the one institution standing between the White House's cheap-money wish and the outcome is still standing.

blocks.text: The court's ruling on the overall path (Db-08, Plausible, 60) is a three-part muddle: captive demand at the short end, passive inflation in the background, and hope for AI growth. None is enough alone. The likeliest exit in 2028 to 2035 is managed financial repression: inflation modestly above coupons, regulatory demand for bills, and a Fed whose leadership becomes more cooperative after 2028. The decoders agree that repression through plumbing has already started (DCC-L1, D1, 70).

blocks.myth: The Fed will simply print money to bail out the Treasury.
blocks.reality: In 2026 the Fed did the opposite and hiked. The quiet help comes from rules that make others buy bills, and from inflation running above the average cost of the debt. That is repression through plumbing, not printing.

blocks.q: Why does a rising share of short-term bills make the system more fragile?
blocks.a: Because bills reprice within months, so any rate rise hits the budget fast, and because the new buyers of bills are leveraged and price-sensitive. When stress comes, they sell or demand higher yields at the worst moment.

chapters.title: The players and what they want
chapters.kicker: Intent and outcome are different things. Most players want more than they can get, and the gap shows where the real limits are.

blocks.text: This chapter separates two questions that news coverage usually blends: what does each player want, and what are they actually getting? Wanting is graded with the decoding scale (D1 strong to D4 debunked). Getting is read from money moved and laws passed.
Trump: a landlord's monetary system

Trump has run one economic worldview for almost 40 years. His paid newspaper letter of 1987-09-02 already said "It's time for us to end our vast deficits by making Japan, and others who can afford it, pay", complained of "a weak yen against a strong dollar", and ended "Tax these wealthy nations, not America." The decoders found four stable wants. In one line: the dollar is the rent everyone must pay, money is cheap for the landlord, and the tenants cover the costs.

blocks.text: Bessent: the trader in the Treasurer's chair

Bessent is the architect of captive demand. He chose the 1863 analogy, said access to the dollar is "no longer unconditional", welcomed "money flow out of some countries of concern" into Treasuries, and called the current system fiat in July 2026. His signal-heavy style (the photographed note, "I am the house now") moves markets more than his money does. The literal "he sold France" story is Refuted (85). The narrow "he chose to let the euro area absorb the shock" version is Plausible (50).
Warsh: the independent hawk, for now

Warsh hiked against the President, citing 65 months of elevated inflation and hyperscaler competition for capital. He has floated the idea of a new Fed-Treasury accord. The decoders give a crisis-era accord and Fed yield support after the 2028 leadership turnover only D2 (40 by 2032). Markets price the Powell governor seat vacated by early 2028 at 64% to 72%. That date is a fork point for the whole story.
Musk: belief yes, project no

Musk has said since 2023 that money is "a database for resource allocation" and on 2026-10-20 that "currency will be measured in ... wattage and tonnage." The decoders rate this a sincere belief (D1, 75) that also works as a valuation story for his energy, AI and launch businesses (D1, 70). Their best reading is both at once (65). But he has built nothing that would make energy money real.

chapters.title: The rails: Set 1 absorbs Set 2
chapters.kicker: New digital money is being built on top of the old system, by law. It is an acquisition, not a merger.

blocks.text: The owner framed the money world as two sets. Set 1 is gold, bonds and bank credit. Set 2 is crypto, Bitcoin, stablecoins and blockchains, used more and more by AI for commerce. His hypothesis was that both survive and merge into "a new monopoly board". The project's ruling (Db-10, Plausible, 65): right in shape, wrong in one important way. Set 2's rails are being absorbed onto Set 1's balance sheet. Set 1 is buying Set 2.

blocks.caption: Four layers of money. Token rails on top move and settle the money. Treasuries and bank deposits underneath are what it is backed by. Gold sits at the bottom as the neutral asset between nations.

blocks.text: Set 1 is three jobs, not one layer

items: Gold is the neutral reserve with no issuer, mostly for states.
Treasuries are the prime collateral that everything else is priced against.
Banks create most credit, by making loans that create deposits.

blocks.text: Crypto replaces the rails (how money moves and settles), not the balance sheet (what money is backed by). Payments move to tokens first, some deposit funding second, and the reserve role last and only partly (Round 2 Q1, Plausible, 70).
A stablecoin is a tokenized T-bill fund with a payment button

From 2027-01-18 every compliant US stablecoin must hold cash, deposits or Treasury bills of 93 days or less. Holders get zero interest by law. So the float belongs to the issuer and its distributors. Circle's Q2 2026 results show the split: $667.7 million of reserve income on $76.5 billion of average USDC, of which $410.4 million (61.5%) went to distribution partners, mainly Coinbase, leaving $48 million of net income. Across the market the float is worth about $11.7 billion a year at a 4.25% bill rate (model). Tether alone made more than $10 billion in 2025.

blocks.text: This is seigniorage, the profit from issuing money, moved into private hands. The Fed used to send the Treasury large profits ($117 billion in 2015, $107.4 billion in 2021). It stopped in September 2022, because the interest it now pays on bank reserves exceeds what its old bonds earn. Its accumulated shortfall, a "deferred asset", was $233.2 billion on 2026-10-14. Today the cleanest seigniorage in the dollar system goes to stablecoin issuers, whose holders lend to them at zero.
Who really buys the tokens

When stablecoins grew (end 2023 to October 2025, +$174.9 billion), the best estimate is that about two thirds went to holders outside the US (model range 55% to 81%), and about 41% was genuinely new dollar demand from people converting local currency. Offshore USDT is 61% of supply. Per $1 of new token, a foreign new-to-dollar buyer adds about $0.80 of Treasury demand, a switch from a US bank deposit about $0.72, and a switch from a government money fund about $0.30 (model). But for the last twelve months there was no growth at all. Treasury's advisory committee once projected about $2 trillion by 2028. That now needs about +$1.7 trillion in about 26 months from a flat base, and markets give stablecoins above $500 billion before 2027 only 3%.

blocks.caption: Old petrodollar loop and new stablecoin loop. From 1974, oil dollars came back as Treasury purchases. From 2027, foreign savers buying dollar tokens do the same by law. The new loop is real but cyclical: it ran flat for the year to October 2026.

blocks.text: Do deposits leave the banks?

Mostly no. The famous "$6.6 trillion of deposits at risk" was all US transactional deposits at end 2024, a ceiling, not a forecast, and when an issuer buys a bill the seller's bank gets the deposit back. What changes is cost (retail deposits at 0.38% become wholesale money near 4%), and a slice of money creation tilts from bank loans toward Treasury bills, as in the 1863 design.
Borrowing stays with regulated lenders

DeFi lends only against collateral you already own, never against future income. All crypto-backed lending was $56.2 billion in Q2 2026, about 0.4% of the $14.10 trillion of US bank loans. A mortgage, car loan or first business loan needs someone who underwrites your future income and absorbs default, so it comes from a bank or a bank-funded lender through at least 2035, even if the money arrives as a token. Banks are moving upstream: their loans to nonbank lenders rose 19.9% in a year to $2.06 trillion, and nonbanks make about 64% of home purchase loans.
CBDC choices: whose balance sheet holds digital money

rows: Private: statutory ban on a Fed CBDC, GENIUS stablecoins, tokenized deposits (JPMorgan's JPMD live since November 2025), FedNow, proposed Fed "skinny" payment accounts
Public retail option with a holding cap (about €3,000 discussed) and offline privacy, plus a live wholesale bridge (Pontes)
Public retail e-CNY, interest-bearing and bank-distributed from 2026-01-01, used cross-border via mBridge ($55.49B cumulative to November 2025)

blocks.text: The fears map unevenly onto these designs. Greater state visibility is real for every digital option, including "private" stablecoins that must be freezable by law (D1). Programmable limits on general balances in G7 countries are folklore so far (D3, 5 by 2035), though targeted vouchers exist (China's Shenzhen lottery, India's food subsidy). Money that expires is D3 (3). The WEF "Great Reset" as a control plan is D3. Calling GENIUS stablecoins a "backdoor CBDC" is D2 (60) as a description of function.
Why the state keeps Set 1: seigniorage and the freeze button

Every dollar payment ends as a transfer on a ledger the US controls: Fedwire moved $4.59 trillion a day in 2025, CHIPS $2.0 trillion. Foreign central banks keep $2.55 trillion of Treasuries in custody at the New York Fed. That is why one Treasury directive on 2022-02-28 could immobilize Russia's central bank assets held by US persons, and why about €202 billion stayed frozen at Euroclear in June 2026. The power comes from law over the ledger keepers, not from technology. So the state lets new rails grow only on terms that keep both seigniorage and the freeze button (DCD-D01, D1, 80). Stablecoins as a sanctions tool: D1, 85.

blocks.q: If stablecoins grow tenfold, does the US government lose control of money?
blocks.a: Not under current law. Compliant stablecoins must hold Treasury bills, pay holders nothing, settle through a Fed-controlled system and freeze on lawful orders. Growth would create more demand for US debt and more reach for US sanctions. The open risk is offshore tokens outside that regime.

rules: Ask what a new money is backed by and who earns the float. The answer is usually old.
Idle stablecoins pay the issuer, not you.
Rails can change fast. The credit decision stays with whoever underwrites your future income.

connects.how: The GENIUS reserve rule is a pipe in Washington's captive demand system.
Gold is the one corner of the board the US does not issue.
A UHI paid as a stablecoin would hand its float to issuers.

chapters.title: The anchors: gold and Bitcoin
chapters.kicker: Gold is gaining a job between nations. It is not coming back as the thing behind your dollars, and the math of revaluing it is smaller than the stories.

blocks.text: If Set 1 is buying Set 2, what is left outside the dollar board? Two candidates: gold, which states hold, and Bitcoin, which mostly individuals hold. The project tested both against money that moved.
Gold: the neutral corner

Central banks bought 863 tonnes of gold in 2025 and 289 tonnes in Q2 2026, buying into a price about 27% below its January high. Poland and China led. France brought 129 tonnes home. 89% of central banks surveyed expect official gold to rise. Ruling Db-04: gold as the neutral reserve layer, Confirmed, 75. The say and do gaps are real too: Russia sold 22 tonnes, Turkey sold, and the first half of 2026 (345 tonnes) was the weakest since 2022.

Why the buying? US secondary sanctions now reach dollar, digital and gold channels. Russia's case shows both sides: about €202 billion of its euro assets are still immobilized at Euroclear, while its gold held at home was never frozen. But Western markets banned its bars, so Russia now sells gold at home to fund its budget. The decoders grade "weaponized dollar rails push states into gold held at home" D1 (80).

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Fire insurance does not need to be worth as much as your house. It needs to pay out in the one disaster you fear. Gold does not insure the world's debt, most of which is owed and settled in the borrower's own currency. It insures a state's ability to pay abroad when its dollar or euro reserves can be frozen. Against that job it is large: official gold is about $5 trillion against $13.2 trillion of allocated foreign exchange reserves, and at end 2025 prices it was 27% of official reserves, more than Treasuries at 22%.
Gold supply: not running out, not exploding

About 222,600 tonnes of gold exist above ground, worth about $29 trillion. Known reserves (about 61,000 tonnes) would add about 27% to that, and known resources (114,400 tonnes) about 51%. Mines produced a record 3,672 tonnes in 2025, so the stock grows about 1.5% to 1.7% a year and would be about 39% larger by 2050. Asteroids are no answer before then: metal asteroids hold about 1 gram of gold per tonne, so returning 1,000 tonnes would mean processing roughly a billion tonnes of asteroid metal (model). Asteroid gold breaking scarcity: D3.

blocks.caption: Seasons of money, 1870 to 2026. Gold anchored money by law for most of the first century, the anchor was cut in 1971, and since then gold has returned as a reserve that states choose, not a rule they must follow.

blocks.text: The revaluation math

The US holds 261,498,926 ounces of gold, booked at the old statutory price of $42.2222, so $11.04 billion. At the market price of $4,078, the one-off gain from marking it up would be about $1.06 trillion: roughly half of one year's deficit and about 2.7% of the debt. Here is what larger targets would need (model):

rows: 10% of debt held by the public
All debt held by the public

blocks.text: So the popular $10,000 to $20,000 targets match "cover a slice", not "cover the debt". Precedents exist (1934: $20.67 to $35, 1972 to 1973: $38 then $42.22), but each came when gold still anchored the dollar by law. The gain would also be new base money, and with the Fed paying interest on reserves near the bill rate, swapping debt for reserves saves almost no interest. Odds from the judges: formal US revaluation by 2029-01-20 about 10, by 2035 about 15, an official price of $10,000 or more by 2035 about 3. Market gold at or above $10,000 by end 2030 about 20, at or above $20,000 by 2035 about 7.
Why not 10x

The owner brought a belief to this project: gold of about $30 to $50 trillion times a 10x collateral multiplier equals the world's debt, and Bitcoin times 10 could support about $300 trillion. Round 1 audited it. The debt to gold ratio has wandered between 12x and 53x, so "gold times 10 equals debt" is a coincidence of one moment. The multiplier also contradicts the owner's own Bank of England citation: banks create money by lending, not by stacking credit on a gold base. Bitcoin times 10 would imply $1.43 million per coin, and real crypto lending runs at about 0.05x. Gold as "what money is backed by": D4.

blocks.caption: The layers of money. Base money is a Fed liability backed mainly by $4.57 trillion of Treasuries. Bank deposits are created when banks lend. Stablecoins are backed by bills. Gold is a separate asset, not the base under any of them.

blocks.myth: Gold is what the dollar is really backed by.
blocks.reality: The legal gold cover behind Federal Reserve notes ended in 1968, and convertibility ended in 1971. In today's system bonds are what most money is backed by: the Fed's main asset is Treasuries, stablecoins hold bills, and Treasuries are claims on future taxes. Gold is the asset states hold in case that system is turned against them.

blocks.text: Bitcoin: politically blessed, not a reserve

The US holds 198,000 to 328,000 forfeited bitcoin, has bought none, and the White House said on 2026-10-14 that purchases need Congress. The proposed ARMA law bars borrowing against, taxing or pledging federal assets and imposes a 20-year hold. US ETFs hold 1.29 million BTC and Tether 98,933. No G20 central bank holding is established. In 2026 Bitcoin rose while gold fell from May to September, fell in hawkish episodes, and traded in a range of $57.7k to $116k over a year. Ruling Db-05: in H0 Bitcoin is a risk asset with political status and a frozen sovereign stockpile, Confirmed, 80. As a future neutral reserve between nations: Speculative, 20 (by 2050).

Bitcoin is energy-priced, not energy-backed (Da-07, Confirmed, 85). Its difficulty adjustment makes miners' energy spend follow the price, but you cannot redeem a coin for a kilowatt hour. The revealing move was by miners themselves: listed miners signed more than $70 billion of AI and data center contracts, because connected power near fiber now earns more as compute. Stranded remote power still earns most as Bitcoin, the only way to turn it into a globally movable asset.

One correction from the audit: the line often attributed to Putin, that Trump uses crypto to devalue US debt, came from adviser Anton Kobyakov on 2025-09-06 and was about stablecoins. As a devaluation plan it grades D3.

blocks.q: A friend says gold must hit $20,000 to match the debt. What would you say?
blocks.a: No mechanism links gold to the debt. The ratio has wandered from 12x to 53x, gold fell 27% in 2026 while debt rose, and even a US revaluation to $21,100 would only match base money, not the debt. Gold can rise on central bank and investor demand, which is a different story.

rules: Size gold like insurance: a slice for the bad state of the world, not a growth engine.
A revaluation is a one-off accounting gain, not a debt cure.
Watch who buys gold at falling prices. Value-sensitive states buying weakness is the signal.

connects.how: The freeze button on dollar rails is why states want gold at home.
Energy is taking over the old job gold did as a limit on money.
Sanctions and gold buying form one of the clearest cross-area links.

chapters.title: Energy: gold's old job
chapters.kicker: Energy will not replace the dollar you spend. It is replacing the job gold used to do: the scarce physical thing that limits what any money can buy.

blocks.text: This was the project's founding question: will energy (watts, tonnage, compute) replace the value role that gold, then bonds, then credit played? The answer, Plausible at 65, has three parts. Energy fails as money you spend. It succeeds as the real ceiling on output. And it is entering the dollar system as collateral, a "watt-dollar".
Part one: why a kilowatt hour is bad money

blocks.caption: The three jobs of money: medium of exchange, store of value and unit of account. A delivered kilowatt hour scored 1 of 5 on both spending and saving, because it is perishable, tied to a place and getting cheaper over time.

items: No kWh-denominated stablecoin or token of material size exists. Every energy-linked instrument found in 2025 and 2026 settles in dollars (Da-01, energy as spendable money, Refuted through 2050, 5).
A kWh has no single price. In 2026 PJM wholesale power rose 41% while California hit historic lows.

A fixed-kWh unit is unstable in both directions (Da-06, Plausible, 80). Solar modules fell from $132 a watt in 1975 to $0.265 in 2024, so over decades a kWh coin would lose value. In 2026 delivered power got dearer, so right now it would gain. Any fix (cap the units, peg to a share of total energy) turns it back into gold, equity or Bitcoin.
History: every energy currency proposal since Ford's 1921 energy dollar failed.

blocks.text: Part two: energy as the binding constraint

Gold limited money by law until 1971. After that the limit was only political: how much debt markets would absorb. In an AI and robot economy, output scales with delivered power, and power cannot be printed. The evidence is money committed: PJM's capacity auction cleared at its cap twice with a 6,623 MW shortfall ($16.4 billion), and data centers explain about 5,100 MW of the peak rise. Ruling Da-03: Confirmed for H0, 80. The refinement matters: the binding input is deliverable firm power plus a grid connection in specific load regions, not energy in general.

rows: Extra energy needed for +2.26 points of AI growth
about 3% a year, against world primary energy growth of 1.4% in 2025

blocks.text: The AI debt dividend is an energy-supply bet (Dc-10, Plausible, 55). Musk himself said electricity additions grow about 4% a year while chip output grows far faster. If power lags, the AI boom shows up as power-price inflation and higher real interest rates, not as tax revenue that shrinks the debt. That is the link between this chapter and the treadmill in Chapter 2.
Part three: the watt-dollar

blocks.caption: Energy as collateral and ceiling under the dollar. Power plants, data centers, power contracts and GPUs back new dollar loans, while delivered power caps how much real output those dollars can claim.

blocks.text: Energy is also taking a growing share of the job Treasuries do as prime collateral, but inside the dollar. The Hyperion data center financing ($27.3 billion), 55.9 GW of power purchase agreements, and GPU-secured debt of $48.4 billion (by a T4 tracker) all back dollar loans, and the first compute futures settle in dollars. This is the heir of the 1974 petrodollar, when a physical input became a dollar commodity. Ruling Da-02: Plausible, 75. Two corrections keep it from Confirmed: the collateral is mostly the credit of the big tech firms with energy assets as backup, and the recycling half of the petrodollar (foreign surpluses into Treasuries) is not shown. The scale is still small, about a third of the stablecoin float.
Musk's physics currency and the allocation problem

Musk's "currency measured in wattage and tonnage" is substantively the 1930s Technocracy plan for energy certificates, a movement his grandfather Joshua Haldeman belonged to from 1936 to 1941. He names no issuer, redemption rule or supply rule. Ruling Da-05: Speculative, 15, for the far future. The robust part of the analysis is the governance problem: a physics unit is either a market price (just a commodity index priced in some money) or an allocation, in which case someone sets the allotments. In Musk's version the natural allocators would be whoever owns generation, launch and compute. That is a concentration of power far larger than central bank discretion.

Compute as a unit of account between machines is Speculative (Da-04, 25). GPU-hours exist as a contract quantity, but nothing is priced in them, and the machine rail actually scaling is the dollar stablecoin.
Who wins, who loses

The winners are whoever owns firm power and grid connections. People on fixed dollar incomes lose whenever AI demand outruns grid supply (Da-10, Plausible, 60). In the year to September 2026 US energy prices rose 20.4% and real hourly earnings fell 0.7%. No bill anywhere indexes a public transfer to energy or compute. And a tax on watts would not save the budget: 1 cent per kWh on all US electricity would raise about $40 billion, 0.74% of federal receipts.

blocks.myth: Energy will become the new money.
blocks.reality: Energy becomes the new limit and the new collateral, priced in dollars. The sequence the court found: energy as collateral now, energy as an index for bonds or transfers possibly after 2035, and energy as an accounting unit only in a post-scarcity world, where the real question is who controls the allocation.

blocks.q: Why would a currency pegged to one kilowatt hour be a poor savings vehicle over 30 years?
blocks.a: Because solar keeps pushing the cost of energy down. If a kWh gets cheaper faster than other goods, prices in kWh rise, so each coin buys less. A 4% yearly fall in real kWh cost gives about 4.2% yearly inflation in kWh terms.

rules: Energy is the ceiling and the collateral, not the cash.
Ask who owns the firm power and the grid connection. That is where AI's value pools.
A physics money still needs an allocator. Ask who that would be.

connects.how: Gold held this ceiling job by law until 1971.
Rising power costs erode fixed incomes and any cash UHI.
China's control of solar hardware is a direct threat to the watt-dollar.

chapters.title: Labor, robots and a Universal High Income
chapters.kicker: Three tiers behave like two classes. A UHI is limited by rent and the tax base, not by robots, and ownership is what moves people across the line.

blocks.text: Musk has called for a "Universal HIGH INCOME via checks issued by the Federal government." Online voices warn of a "permanent underclass". The owner's own model has three tiers: asset owners, UHI recipients and people still working. This chapter tests all three ideas.
Where the robots really are

Labor's share of nonfarm business income is 52.8%, the lowest since 1947, while unit profits rose 43.0% annualized and unemployment held at 4.2%. But robots are not yet the cause at scale. About 14,500 humanoids shipped worldwide in 2025, about 90% Chinese. 603,307 industrial robots were installed in 2025 with 5 million operating. A fleet of one million humanoids by 2028 is below 10%. Ruling Dc-05: robots are not a macro labor substitute before 2030, Plausible, 85. The pre-2030 effect is software AI on entry-level hiring.

blocks.caption: Three tiers become two classes. Workers and UHI recipients both live on income streams. Owners' income grows with assets. The decisive line is ownership.

blocks.text: Ruling Dd-01: the three tiers collapse into two classes, owners and income-stream dependents, Plausible, 65. Workers and UHI recipients sit in the same structural place relative to capital. Round 2 confirmed the squeeze is shared: both face housing, health cover and, in 2026, energy up 20.4%.
Credit is not the trap. Ownership is.

The owner feared UHI recipients would lose access to credit. Under current law that is Refuted, conditional (Dd-02, 80). Lenders may not discriminate against public-assistance income (ECOA), and Fannie Mae counts income that will continue at least three years. On that basis $1,000 a month supports roughly a $69,000 mortgage (model). The exception is a UHI whose amount politicians reset each year, like Alaska's dividend, which fails the three-year test.

Selling the stream is another matter. Social Security has been non-assignable since 1935 (42 USC 407) for good reason: pension advance firms charged up to 183% APR, and one veteran got $1,500 for $18,000 of pension. A $1,000 monthly stream is worth about $181,000 in present value, but buyers historically paid 30 to 60 cents on the dollar. The real gap is ownership and compounding (Dd-03, Plausible, 70): a borrower capped by debt to income rules on $2,500 a month can buy about $178,000 of housing, while asset prices follow the capital share.
The UHI arithmetic

A $30,000 UHI for about 262 million adults costs about $7.86 trillion a year: 24% of GDP, 106% of all FY2026 outlays and 145% of receipts. Financed by borrowing, it takes debt from 101% of GDP to about 128% in year one, 238% in year five and 374% in year ten at constant rates (Dc-08, Confirmed as arithmetic, 90). Even $10,000 is 8% of GDP and reaches about 211% by year ten. Printing does not escape this in the US: bank reserves earn 3.90%, so money finance is overnight borrowing.

blocks.caption: Nominal versus real value of a UHI. The number on the check stays the same. What it buys depends on how it was financed and on how fast the things it buys can be supplied.

rows: Poverty 38.8% to 27.4%, then inflation of 10.0%, 8.4% and 14.3%. Stopped after the 2012 election
Lost about 58% of real value in five years
about 17% of local GDP, donor dollars

blocks.text: The lesson: small and funded is safe, large and printed is eroded within two to five years. Real value is nominal divided by one plus inflation.
Housing is the limit, not robots

Round 3 found the decisive reason. A UHI dollar is spent about 40% to 48% on housing, and housing supply grows about 1% a year. So even unlimited robot goods can meet at most 57% to 76% of the extra demand. Recalibrated, a printed Musk-scale UHI runs about 5.8% to 9.8% inflation now, 1.4% to 5.8% in 2028 to 2035 and 0.3% to 2.7% after 2035 (model, and a lower bound because it has no interest channel). Round 2's 0.9% case needs housing supply to open first. A UHI of 10% of GDP is much easier: about 1.5% to 3.9% now.

A printed UHI would feel generous on gadgets and food and thin on rent within two to three years. In nearly every model case, shelter is 50% to 100% of the demand left unmet. Robots make the goods. Landlords capture the checks.
The tax base is moving the wrong way

Treasuries are claims on future taxes, and those taxes rest on wages. In FY2026 individual income and payroll taxes carried 86.2% of federal receipts, and corporate tax only 7.1%, down from 10.8% in FY2024, as firms expensed AI investment (Microsoft's current tax bill fell from $14.1 billion to $2.5 billion). Each point of labor share lost costs about 0.8% of receipts. Ruling R3-3: the tax base shifting to capital, energy or compute is Refuted for now (70). A 5% excise on hyperscaler capex would raise about $35 billion. The big money is in taxing capital income and equity, not watts or tokens.
What is actually on the table

No federal UHI or AI dividend bill has moved past introduction, and none found is money financed. Sanders' bill takes a one-time 50% stake in large AI firms and pays about $1,000 per person, which needs a $3.2 to $6.8 trillion stake (model). Inside the administration, Bessent reportedly prefers AI equity seeded into Trump Accounts. Working odds by 2035: a cash UHI or AI dividend about 10, AI equity routed into accounts or a public fund about 25. Five states ban local guaranteed income. The first "AI dividend" you see is more likely a locked account for your child than a monthly check.

blocks.q: Why can robots not make a large printed UHI non-inflationary on their own?
blocks.a: Because almost half of UHI spending goes to housing, which robots cannot multiply quickly. Housing supply grows about 1% a year, so the unmet demand piles up there and shows up as rent and price inflation.

rules: A UHI check is worth what it buys. Divide by one plus inflation.
Count it as income, never sell the stream.
Size any transfer to the housing you can deliver, not to the robot forecast.

connects.how: A deficit-financed UHI turns the treadmill explosive.
Housing and ownership decide what the next generation can reach.
Rent, tax base and power prices link this chapter to the debt.

chapters.title: The next generation
chapters.kicker: The ladder was not pulled up. One rung broke, one got cheap but lottery-like, and ownership decides the climb.

blocks.text: The owner's deepest worry was about children: when a child turns 18 in this new world, is the classic route still open? Labor to cash, then credit backed by income, then a home or a business. The project's answer (Round 2 Q6, Plausible, 70): yes, but it has changed shape.

blocks.caption: The ladder from first job to owning assets. The first job rung still holds. The housing rung broke for entrants since 2020. A new side ladder, launching a brand, got cheap but steep.

blocks.text: Rung one: the first job still exists

Unemployment for ages 20 to 24 was 8.0% in September 2026, down from 9.2% a year earlier. The bend is in AI-exposed white-collar entry roles: recent graduates aged 22 to 27 had 5.6% unemployment against 4.2% for all workers, which used to be the other way round, and the entry share of postings in exposed jobs fell from nearly 60% in 2020 to 44.7%. The facts are Confirmed (80). AI as the main cause only Plausible (55), because rates and post-2021 overhiring are rival explanations.
Rung two: the housing rung broke

The median first-time buyer is now a record 40 years old, and first-time buyers are a record 21% of sales. For a 20 to 24-year-old saving 10% of pay, a 10% down payment on a median existing home took about 6.2 years in 1990 and about 10.0 years now (model, with the 1990 price a memory figure to verify). The monthly payment on a median home went from about 40 to about 68 hours of work since early 2020. 49% of adults under 30 live with a parent. The gate is the down payment, not the monthly payment.

blocks.caption: Hours of work needed, then versus now. Since 1990 food at home got 24% cheaper in hours and quality-adjusted cars 54% cheaper. A median home, a family health premium and public tuition got dearer.

blocks.text: This is the honest version of the movie "In Time", where the poor run out of time. Goods got cheaper in hours of work, entry assets got dearer. Of the $78.1 trillion rise in US household wealth since late 2019, the top 10% took 67.5% and the bottom half 3.1%. A price index tracks groceries, not a first home, so a CPI-indexed wage or UHI keeps up with food and falls behind on shelter.
Can robots and zoning fix housing?

Only together. Land is 68.4% of single-family home value in San Jose and 39.9% nationally. So a 20% cut in building cost lowers prices about 6% in San Jose and about 16% in St. Louis (model). Factory building has a hard record: Katerra burned through more than $2 billion before its 2021 bankruptcy, and robots are under 0.03% of global construction spend. Broad zoning works: Auckland's 2016 upzoning doubled construction, and Austin's median rent fell from $1,546 to $1,296. Narrow reforms do little: Minneapolis's triplex rule produced 47 homes in five years. Ruling R3-5: Plausible, 65, sooner in the Sun Belt, later on the coasts.
Rung three: launching got cheap, staying visible got dear

A digital brand can launch for about $525 to $2,850 and a small physical brand for about $1,900 to $7,400 (model). Solo founders are a record 63% of Stripe Atlas companies. But median solo founder revenue fell 23% in 2025 while the top decile earned 61 times the median. Family money is the real seed round: 47% of 18 to 29-year-olds got outside help.

blocks.caption: Where $10 of a mass cosmetic goes. Product cost is about $1.76, the retailer keeps about $4.00, marketing about $1.47, other costs about $2.30 and profit about $0.27. A strong robot and energy shock saves maybe 36 cents.

blocks.text: The tolls are rising. Amazon's advertising went from 23.5% to 41.9% of its seller services revenue (2019 to H1 2026), Etsy's take rate from 16.5% to 24.2%, and Meta's price per ad rose 12% to 14% a year in 2026 (R3-7, Confirmed, 70). A human-made premium is real as a label effect in experiments but not yet measured as a cash price (Plausible, 55). Buying a founder's community is the modern exit: the brand rhode added $293.5 million of sales in its first year inside e.l.f.
Child accounts: real, but measured in tenths of a point

cols: Trump Account at 18, 5% real, today's dollars

blocks.text: The seed covers births from 2025 to 2028, so the first seeded cohort turns 18 in 2043. At 18 the account becomes IRA-like, with education and a $10,000 first-home exception but no business exception. The bottom half of households hold 0.58% of directly held equities, a floor since 2010 after a 1996 peak of 1.65%. Trump Accounts as designed lift that to about 0.60% to 0.70% by 2045. Only a grant of about $500 billion of AI equity reaches about 1.27% (R3-11, Plausible, 70). The SEED OK trial showed what works: automatic deposits, not sign-ups.

blocks.q: Why does the "permanent underclass" meme get the mechanism right but the conclusion wrong?
blocks.a: It is right that ownership decides outcomes. It is wrong that the door is shut. The route becomes permanent only if three things persist: asset returns beating wages, blocked housing supply, and ownership grants too small to matter.

rules: Build a credit file early, live cheaply, and own diversified assets from the first paycheck. General information, not advice.
Launch cheaply, but budget for attention. The factory is cheap, the shelf is not.
For housing, rezoning votes matter more than robot news.

connects.how: The two-class split is what the 18-year-old is trying to cross.
Land and platform tolls catch the savings robots create.
The epilogue follows a child born today to 2050.

chapters.title: The rivals and the shocks
chapters.kicker: The rivals' strongest card is hardware, not currency. The shocks that matter in 2026 came from oil, the yen and Paris.

blocks.text: A popular story says rivals will dethrone the dollar with a BRICS currency or a Treasury fire sale. The project scored every lever with one formula (cost to the US, times likelihood, times how cheap the move is for the rival, divided by 25) and found the money levers weak. BRICS agreed on no currency in New Delhi in September 2026 (score 0.12). A Treasury fire sale would hurt China most (0.08). mBridge has handled about $55 billion in total (0.60).
China: Treasury can issue bills, not magnets

Proposed 16 October 2026: 40 technologies, 12 of them solar, including wafers of 70 micrometers or less. Finished panels excluded. Comments close 15 November
Political truce extended to 10 January 2027, but the legal end date stays 10 November 2026
Thin yuan leg: 94% of Chinese energy loans in 2010 to 2021 were in dollars
China supplied 50% of US lithium-ion imports by value
At least two tankers paid Hormuz tolls in yuan

blocks.text: The court's odds for 10 November: a numbered extension 72%, partial replacement 16%, full lapse 12%. The solar know-how ban finalized in some form: about 25% by end 2026 and about 70% by mid-2027. China holds above 94% of polysilicon and 97% of wafer capacity. Its strategy is precise: sell panels, keep the factories. If the October package lapses with no replacement, the project moves 2 points from S1 to S4 for 2028.
The battery swap

Electric freight moves goods prices away from dollar oil, but into a different chokepoint. China makes over 80% of battery cells, about 85% of cathode and more than 90% of anode material. On a concentration index, battery mid-stream stages score about 5,250 to 9,400, against oil's 830 to 906 by country. But oil is a flow and a battery is a stock: cut off oil and trucks stop within weeks, cut off batteries and only new vehicles and the 8% to 12% of packs replaced each year are exposed (R3-12, Plausible, 70). The country electrifying fastest is China itself: new-energy heavy trucks were 38.1% of sales in January to September 2026, a hedge against its own Hormuz exposure.
The 2026 shocks

items: Hormuz. A war closed the strait in practice. Brent reached $115.22 and US diesel $6.276 a gallon, up 73% in a year. War-risk insurance jumped to 3.5% to 7.5% of hull value per transit from 0.10% to 0.25%. Markets give normal traffic before 2028 about 48%. The freight spike adds roughly 1 point to CPI, peaking about a year later.
The yen. USD/JPY neared 164 in July. Japan spent ¥27.1 trillion defending it in 2026 and the Bank of Japan hiked on 18 September. Today it is 157.10, below the 160 to 164 intervention zone.

France. The France to Germany spread went from 87 to 157.5 basis points between 10 September and 21 October. Tripwires are 175 (ECB adjustments) and 200 (its TPI backstop). Markets put a Le Pen presidency in 2027 at about 46. Moody's decision on France's Aa3 negative rating was due after the close on 23 October: thin markets said 87.5% for a downgrade by 31 October, the court about 70.

blocks.text: When the dollar is strong, the US exports inflation. In 2022 the IMF estimated a 10% dollar rise passes about 1 point of inflation to other countries. In 2026 the absorbers were oil importers with weak currencies: the rupee near 96.9, the Philippine peso past 60, the rupiah at 17,315. But the US was not insulated either: energy CPI rose 20.4%. The court's conclusion: the US can export inflation or weaken the dollar to help industry, not both at once.

chapters.title: Connecting the dots: the interconnection map
chapters.kicker: Information arbitrage: the most useful insights sit between topics, where a cause in one area quietly drives an effect in another.

blocks.text: Most coverage treats debt, crypto, energy, housing and geopolitics as separate beats. The research kept finding the same few pipes running through all of them. This chapter lists the links that are easiest to miss when each topic is read alone. Each is one cause, one effect and the evidence that ties them. Together they explain why a closure of a strait in the Gulf can raise a young American's mortgage rate, and why AI investment can weaken the collateral under the world's money.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Think of a city's water system. Houses, factories and fountains look separate, but they all hang off the same mains. A burst pipe across town drops your shower pressure. In the money system the mains are Treasury bills, delivered power and land. Almost every link below runs through one of them.
Fourteen links

items: Hormuz oil drives the French bond spread: the France to Germany spread was flat in August and blew out from 87 to 157.5 basis points only after Brent passed $100, alongside the Fed and Bank of Japan hikes, which is why the project now sees the likeliest near-term disorderly path as oil-shock inflation with the euro periphery as the weak link.

Japan's yen defense feeds into US mortgage rates: instead of borrowing through the unused FIMA line, foreign official holders sold $254 billion of Treasuries in 2026, and the 10-year yield went from 4.68% on 30 July to 5.13% in October.

AI investment weakens the collateral under money: firms expensing AI capex cut corporate tax to 7.1% of receipts while wages carry 86.2%, so Treasuries rest more on a labor share that is already at a record low 52.8%, which moved one point from S1 to S4 for 2035 to 2050.

Data centers drive household budgets: PJM capacity cleared at its cap with a 6,623 MW shortfall, wholesale power there rose 41%, and US energy prices rose 20.4% while real hourly earnings fell 0.7%, so the AI boom is already taxing every fixed income, including any future UHI.

China's solar know-how ban targets the watt-dollar: if AI output is capped by delivered power, the country that controls 97% of wafer capacity holds a lever over the dollar's new collateral, which is why solar technology controls now top the threat table at 3.00.

Stablecoin law ties crypto to the bill market: the 93-day reserve rule means every compliant token is a buyer of Treasury bills, so crypto's boom and bust cycle now feeds straight into the Treasury's funding, as the flat $304 billion year showed.

Low interest rates would break private seigniorage: Circle's model stops covering costs at a bill yield of about 1.5%, so a future rate-cutting cycle would push issuers to cut distributor payouts and fold into banks, concentrating the new rails in fewer hands.

A bill-heavy debt makes the Fed a budget actor: with 22.36% of marketable debt in bills and 35.7% repricing within a year, each hike reaches the federal interest bill within months, which raises the political pressure on Fed appointments after 2028.

Sanctions drive gold: the freezing of about €202 billion of Russian euro assets, while its gold at home stayed untouched, is the clearest reason central banks bought 863 tonnes in 2025 and France brought 129 tonnes home.

Conditional crisis access pushes toward neutral reserves: the Gulf asked for swap lines and got none announced, borrowing a record $102.7 billion instead, a small push that moved one point toward S2 for 2028 to 2035.

Land prices cap both UHI and the robot dividend: shelter takes 40% to 48% of UHI spending and land is 68.4% of home value in San Jose, so robot-built savings and printed checks both end up as land rent unless zoning lets more homes share the land.

Platform tolls absorb automation's savings: a strong robot and energy shock saves about 36 cents on a $10 cosmetic while Amazon's ads rose to 41.9% of seller services revenue, so cheaper production reaches shoppers slowly and founders' margins shrink.

Interest on the debt flows upward: net interest of $1.05 trillion goes mostly to the top decile, who hold 79% of household-held government securities, while the bottom half owes 51.6% of consumer credit, so a rising interest bill widens the wealth gap on its own.

Fed losses turn printing into borrowing: since the Fed pays 3.90% on reserves and carries a $233.2 billion deferred asset, a money-financed UHI or a gold revaluation gain becomes interest-bearing reserves, so neither escapes the debt arithmetic.

The state keeps money anchored to bills it can sell and taxes it can raise. Those taxes fall on wages. The interest on those bills flows to owners. So the plumbing that keeps the dollar strong is also the plumbing that widens the gap, unless ownership itself is spread.

Any plan that ignores interest on reserves or land rent is missing half its cost.
The plumbing that protects the currency can widen the wealth gap. Both are true at once.

chapters.title: Epilogue: the most probable path from here
chapters.kicker: Not a prophecy. The single most likely story the evidence supports, the dates where it could fork, and what it means for you.

blocks.text: Odds tell you which endings are likely. They do not tell you a story. This epilogue does, by following the most likely mix of scenarios from late 2026 to 2050. It is a judgment built on the project's rulings, so by the project's own rules it is Speculative. Every number in it comes from the research. The shape is the one the Round 1 judge drew and Round 3 kept: dollar plumbing grows, a repression episode is run partly through that plumbing, and gold's neutral role expands quietly underneath.

blocks.caption: One road splitting into four scenarios. The thickest branch through 2028 is dollar extension (62), with a disorderly reset (22) as the main alternative. By 2050 the branches are almost even between dollar extension (31), disorderly reset (31) and a neutral reserve layer (28).

blocks.text: Act one, 2026 to 2028: the pipes switch on while the oil burns

The next few weeks are crowded with tests: Moody's on France (23 October), the Fed (28 October), Q3 GDP (29 October), the midterms (3 November), the Treasury refunding (4 November), the Cook hearing (5 November), China's legal deadline on rare earths (10 November) and the Fed again (9 December, a hike priced at 75% to 79%). Most likely, China extends (72%), the Fed hikes into an oil shock, and the Treasury keeps leaning on bills.

On 18 January 2027 the GENIUS rules switch on, and every compliant dollar token becomes a buyer of Treasury bills by law. The rails are built, but they do not carry much yet: supply is flat near $304 billion and markets give $500 billion before 2027 only 3%. The Fed and money funds keep doing the heavy lifting. Oil keeps inflation sticky while Hormuz stays a coin flip (normal before 2028: about 48%). The weak link is the euro periphery, with France's spread watched against 175 and 200 basis points and a Le Pen presidency priced near 46% for 2027. At the end of this act the likeliest description is still dollar extension (62). The main alternative is an oil-shock inflation and term-premium episode met by a Fed that hikes (22). The chance of a bond-market episode forcing the Fed to act at all in this period: about 30.
Act two, 2028 to 2035: the quiet squeeze

This is the act where the treadmill speeds up on its own. About 70% of the marketable debt reprices at market rates within five years, and if yields hold, interest heads to about $1.6 trillion within three years and $1.9 trillion within five. The Powell governor seat is likely vacated by early 2028 (priced 64% to 72%), and Trump's term ends on 20 January 2029. A more cooperative Fed is the hinge.

The most likely result is managed financial repression, the 1940s and 1970s hybrid the decoders identified: inflation modestly above the average coupon, rules that make banks, funds and token issuers hold bills, and perhaps Fed support at the long end. Not Weimar, not default (judged below 5%). The judges' odds by 2035: a bond episode forcing Fed balance sheet action 45, an explicit yield cap or Fed-Treasury accord 25, inflation above 5% for two straight years 25, a gold revaluation 12 to 15, a coercive restructuring 4, capital controls on US residents 7.

Meanwhile the edges move. The US CBDC ban reaches its sunset on 31 December 2030, but a Fed retail CBDC by 2035 is only about 7, because private tokens already do the job. The digital euro probably arrives around 2029 to 2030 (about 50 by end 2030). States keep buying gold at home because dollar access now comes with conditions. China's hardware leverage shapes the price of solar, batteries and EVs more than the currency you are paid in. A cash UHI or AI dividend by 2035 stays unlikely (about 10). AI equity routed into child accounts or a public fund is more likely (about 25). End of act: dollar extension 44, disorderly reset 30, neutral reserve layer 23, energy standard 3.
Act three, 2035 to 2050: who owns the output

By now the question is no longer the rails. It is the tax base. If the labor share keeps falling from 52.8% while wages still carry most federal receipts, the collateral under the world's money weakens slowly, which is why dollar extension and disorderly reset end tied at 31. Gold's stock grows about 1.6% a year and is about 39% larger by 2050, still scarce, still neutral, with a neutral reserve layer at 28. Energy may become an index for some bonds or transfers. An energy or compute standard reaches 10 only because machine economies could be large by then, and any energy unit still needs a scarcity rule that pulls it back toward gold or Bitcoin.

The first child seeded with a Trump Account turns 18 in 2043. On current design the bottom half's share of equities rises from 0.58% to only about 0.60% to 0.70% by 2045. Whether that child inherits the two-class world depends on choices made in act two: by-right housing, ownership grants at a scale relative to asset prices, and taxing capital income rather than watts.

rows: The choice is not whether losses happen but who carries them and how visibly. Size any UHI to housing supply, tax capital income rather than watts, auto-deposit child accounts, and fund battery mid-stream materials and firm power

blocks.text: The dollar most likely survives this period, not because it is strong but because the state has wired the new money to its own debt. The cost of that survival is paid quietly, through inflation above savings rates, rent, and a tax base resting on wages. The one force that changes who pays is ownership. That is the thread that ties the whole landscape together.

blocks.q: In the most likely path, what does a "disorderly reset" look like for an American household?
blocks.a: Not a bank holiday or a new currency. Several years of prices rising faster than pay and savings rates, while the government quietly benefits as its debt shrinks in real terms. Fixed-rate mortgages and real assets hold up, long-term cash savings lose.

rules: The likeliest US reset is slow repression, not a crash. Plan for years, not days.
Watch dates and tripwires, not predictions. The fork points are on the calendar.
Ownership is the only lever that changes who pays.

rulebook.rule: The debt's engine is the primary deficit, not the interest rate.
rulebook.why: At market rates the primary deficit ($940.7B, 2.92% of GDP) explains 92% to 102% of the yearly rise in the debt ratio. Real rates sit only 0.26 points above trend growth.

rulebook.rule: Washington manages who must buy the debt, not how big it is.
rulebook.why: Bills, bank rule relief, buybacks and the stablecoin reserve rule all create captive buyers. Captive demand is Confirmed (75). No one in power is using gold, Bitcoin or default.

rulebook.rule: New money rails sit on old assets.
rulebook.why: From 2027-01-18 every compliant dollar token must hold Treasury bills of 93 days or less. Set 1 is buying Set 2, not merging with it.

rulebook.rule: Idle cash and zero-yield tokens pay someone else.
rulebook.why: $50,000 earns about $2,125 a year in bills, $190 in average savings and $0 from a stablecoin issuer. The float is private seigniorage.

rulebook.rule: An announced backstop is not a used one.
rulebook.why: The Fed's FIMA line sat at zero from February to October 2026 while foreign governments sold $254B of Treasuries. Check the weekly balance sheet, not the press release.

rulebook.rule: Gold is insurance between states, not the backing of your dollar.
rulebook.why: Central banks bought 863t in 2025 because dollar rails can be frozen. The gold to debt ratio has wandered from 12x to 53x, so no formula links them.

rulebook.rule: Energy is the ceiling and the collateral, not the cash.
rulebook.why: Delivered power now limits AI output (PJM cleared at its cap, 6,623 MW short), and power assets back dollar loans. A kWh coin fails as money because it is perishable, local and getting cheaper.

rulebook.rule: A UHI check is worth what it buys, and housing decides what it buys.
rulebook.why: 40% to 48% of UHI spending goes to shelter, whose supply grows about 1% a year. A printed Musk-scale UHI runs about 5.8% to 9.8% inflation today.

rulebook.rule: Count a benefit as income. Never sell the stream.
rulebook.why: Lenders must count steady public income, about $69k of mortgage per $1,000 a month. Buyers of benefit streams have paid 30 to 60 cents on the dollar, at APRs up to 183%.

rulebook.rule: Ownership, not income, decides who keeps up.
rulebook.why: The top 10% took 67.5% of the $78.1T rise in household wealth since late 2019. The bottom half hold 0.58% of directly held stocks.

rulebook.rule: Cheap production does not reach you on its own.
rulebook.why: Land takes the savings where it is most of a home's value (68.4% in San Jose), and platforms take a rising slice of each sale (Amazon ads 41.9% of seller services).

rulebook.rule: Rivals' real lever is hardware, not currency.
rulebook.why: Solar technology controls score 3.00 on the threat table, a BRICS currency 0.12. The Treasury can issue bills, but it cannot issue a magnet.

rulebook.rule: The likeliest US reset is slow repression, not a crash.
rulebook.why: The reserve issuer borrows in its own currency, so the loss arrives as years of inflation above coupons and savings rates. Explicit default is judged below 5%.

rulebook.rule: Grade intent and outcome separately, and follow money over words.
rulebook.why: Trump's cheap-money want is D1 but he is not getting it. Musk's energy money is a sincere belief with nothing built. The say and do gap is the most valuable data.

questions.q: Who actually holds dollar stablecoins, country by country?
questions.a: Nobody publishes it. The Fed's September 2026 note says chain data lack geography, and Tether reports 650 million users with no country split. The project's model puts about two thirds of growth-phase supply abroad (range 55% to 81%). The first hard test is the 2028-07-18 ban on non-permitted coins for US persons.

questions.q: Is the 2026 rise in real interest rates driven by AI capital demand or by oil, Japan and term premium?
questions.a: The real 10-year yield rose 82 basis points in 2026 to 2.76%, now above the 2.5% real growth line. No decomposition exists yet. It matters most of all, because if AI pushes real rates up one for one with growth, the AI dividend does nothing for the debt (129% of GDP either way).

questions.q: Will the 2028 Fed leadership turnover bring a Fed-Treasury accord on yields?
questions.a: Warsh has floated the idea of a new accord, and markets price the Powell governor seat vacated by early 2028 at 64% to 72%. The decoders grade yield support after the turnover D2, about 40 by 2032. An explicit cap or accord by 2035 is judged about 25.

questions.q: Does the corporate tax collapse reverse when AI capex growth slows?
questions.a: Corporate receipts fell 15.6% in FY2026 to $381.4B as firms expensed investment, and corporate tax is now 7.1% of receipts. The skeptic's case is that this is a timing effect that reverses. The test is the corporate share climbing back above 10% while capex keeps growing.

questions.q: Next time Japan defends the yen, will it borrow through FIMA or sell Treasuries again?
questions.a: In 2026 it said it planned to use FIMA and did not. Foreign official custody fell $254B to $2,549.1B. The tripwires are a FIMA draw above $1B during an intervention and custody below $2.5T. USD/JPY is 157.10, below the 160 to 164 intervention zone.

questions.q: Do Gulf states get dollar lines from the Treasury, and on what conditions?
questions.a: The UAE asked in April, Bessent pointed to the Exchange Stabilization Fund (about $219B), and no line was announced by 22 October. The ESF monthly statements were not read, so a quiet line cannot be ruled out. Conditional access is the small push behind S2 gaining a point.

questions.q: Does conditional dollar access show up in central bank gold buying?
questions.a: The link is inference so far, which is why the court moved only one point toward a neutral reserve layer. The WGC's Q3 2026 data, due in late October or early November, is the next check. Above 200 tonnes a quarter would confirm.

questions.q: How fast can US housing supply actually respond in the 2020s?
questions.a: This is the single input that most limits any UHI and any robot dividend, and the project lacks a 2020s supply elasticity. Broad upzoning worked in Auckland and Austin. Narrow reforms produced little. FHFA land shares after 2022 are also missing.

questions.q: Will China pair its solar know-how ban with yuan finance for the Global South?
questions.a: So far the yuan leg is thin: 94% of Chinese energy loans in 2010 to 2021 were in dollars and the Global South solar boom is bought for cash. The yuan grows by refinancing old debt instead, as in Kenya, where its share of external debt rose from 5% to 11.7%.

questions.q: Is there a real cash premium for human-made goods?
questions.a: Experiments show a label effect on ratings and purchase intent, and a preregistered auction study finds bids fall as AI involvement rises, but its effect size was not seen. No transaction-based estimate exists, and platforms such as Etsy capture part of any premium.

questions.q: Why was producer price inflation for finished consumer goods flat in 2026 while energy CPI rose 20.4%?
questions.a: Unresolved. Both are official series as published. The likely cause is the energy weight and coverage of the producer series. It matters because it decides how much of the 2026 shock is still in the pipeline for 2027.

questions.q: If a UHI or AI dividend law passes, will payments be pledgeable or programmable?
questions.a: No bill found makes payments assignable, tokenized or programmable, and none is money-financed. A cash UHI written into the Social Security Act would inherit its anti-assignment rule. The Sanders bill's payment mechanics and any CBO score are still to be read.
